body.text: The qualifying income limit was a former SR&ED test in Canada that reduced a Canadian-controlled private corporation's (CCPC's) expenditure limit when prior-year taxable income exceeded it. Budget 2019 eliminated this test, so the enhanced 35% refundable ITC expenditure limit is phased out only by prior-year taxable capital or, after December 15, 2024, an elective three-year average gross revenue test.

Canada operates a comprehensive, two-tiered research and development (R&D) tax incentive system anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program under the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and complemented by provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and direct innovation grants. Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant statutory overhaul in over a decade. Following initial proposals in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded commitments in the November 4, 2025 federal budget presented by Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne, Parliament enacted Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million (yielding up to $2.1 million annually in refundable ITCs), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

At the provincial level, parallel legislative reforms have reshaped sub-national R&D tax planning across key jurisdictions. In its March 25, 2025 budget, Québec abolished seven legacy R&D and innovation tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating its regime into the fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), which provides an increased rate of 30% on the first $1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold (regardless of corporate asset size) and a basic rate of 20% on excess expenditures. In Western Canada, British Columbia's 2026 budget made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent and extended refundability to ECPCs to mirror the federal Bill C-15 reforms. Meanwhile, judicial decisions from the Federal Court of Appeal and the Tax Court of Canada through 2026—including Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. (2021 FCA 88), National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72), Dazzm Inc. (2024 TCC 129), Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. (2025 TCC 173), Tuna Temple Inc. (2025 TCC 183), and Willowglen Systems Inc. (2026 TCC 7)—confirm that while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) streamlined its administrative guidance into a "Why" and "How" framework and launched an eight-week elective pre-claim approval process, the five-factor common law test from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) and the mandatory 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline remain strictly enforced.
1. Executive Summary and 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program delivers two distinct, interlocking statutory tax incentives for taxpayers carrying on business in Canada that perform or fund eligible R&D within Canada. First, under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers accumulate allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures in a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, which may be deducted against business income in the current taxation year or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future years. Second, under subsections 127(5) to 127(36) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers earn an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on their annual "qualified expenditures" at either an enhanced rate of 35% (for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations, up to their annual expenditure limit) or a basic rate of 15% (for all other corporations, unincorporated individuals, partnerships, trusts, and CCPC or ECPC expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit). Unused ITCs that are not refunded in cash (at 100% or 40%, depending on claimant type and expenditure nature) may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Part I tax otherwise payable.

Auditors, corporate tax directors, and legal advisers evaluating multi-year claims must distinguish three major federal legislative enactments between 2024 and 2026 that govern expenditure eligibility, government assistance reductions, and credit rates. First, Bill C-69 (Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on June 20, 2024, amended the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act effective retroactively to January 1, 2020 (applicable to loans made after December 31, 2019). Under Bill C-69, bona fide loans with reasonable repayment arrangements received from public authorities in Canada—defined as "excluded loans" under subsection 12(11)—are no longer treated as government assistance and therefore do not reduce a claimant's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures or qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Affected taxpayers were permitted to file amended returns with a revised Form T661 for any non-statute-barred taxation year beginning after 2019.

Second, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) (released in draft legislation by the Department of Finance Canada on August 15, 2025, with stakeholder consultation through September 12, 2025) proposed the foundational modernization of the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. The 2024 FES initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $4.5 million (which would have provided up to $1.575 million in annual refundable ITCs), increasing the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), permitting CCPCs to elect to use the gross revenue phase-out structure in lieu of taxable capital, and restoring SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Third, the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget and Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted the 2024 FES structural reforms into law while further increasing the annual expenditure limit from the FES-proposed $4.5 million to $6.0 million, effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Following Royal Assent of Bill C-15, the Canada Revenue Agency issued updated versions of Form T661 (May 15, 2026), Form T1145 and Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), T2 Schedule 31 (May 22, 2026), and T2 Schedule 49 (May 29, 2026), alongside revised administrative policies on Shared-Use Equipment and Total Qualified Expenditures (May 22, 2026), Lease Expenditures (June 8, 2026), Capital Expenditures (June 29, 2026), and Investment Tax Credits (October 7, 2026).

body.text: 2. Federal Statutory Architecture and Scientific Eligibility Framework
2.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The foundational threshold for all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is undertaken in one of three core categories of work, expanded by directly linked support work and restricted by statutory exclusions:

items: Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Small businesses account for 65% of all SR&ED claims submitted to the CRA (based on 2025–2026 fiscal year statistics), with experimental development representing the primary stream for commercial and industrial claimants.

body.text: 2.2 The CRA Eligibility Guidelines ("Why" and "How" Methodology) vs. The Common Law Five-Question Test

For nearly three decades, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), and the CRA evaluated SR&ED project eligibility under the common law five-question test formulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC). In the 2015 version of its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, the CRA codified a two-step administrative review methodology. Step 1 ("Determine if there is SR&ED") required answering five sequential questions in the affirmative, while Step 2 ("Determine the extent of eligible work") identified commensurate support work and excluded commercial or routine tasks:

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: On August 16, 2021, the CRA archived its prior policy and published the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. Designed to simplify pre-application self-assessments for businesses, the 2021 Guidelines consolidated the eligibility analysis into two fundamental questions—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement.

Under the "Why" Requirement, the claimant must establish why the work is being conducted: it must be undertaken to advance scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. Achieving a technological advancement requires overcoming a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty—a limitation in the current state of scientific or technological knowledge that cannot be resolved using publicly available knowledge, routine engineering, or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field. Both the CRA and the courts distinguish true technological uncertainty from routine technical debugging, commercial/business risk, or apprenticeship-level learning curves where an employee lacks standard training in the field (as held in Chagnon, 2023 TCC 35). However, under Northwest Hydraulic and recent software and manufacturing jurisprudence (Buhler, 2023 TCC 18; Dazzm Inc., 2024 TCC 129; Willowglen Systems Inc., 2026 TCC 7), "system uncertainty" is fully eligible where known technologies, open-source frameworks, or sub-assemblies interact in complex ways whose systemic behaviour cannot be predicted by competent professionals using standard procedures. Furthermore, as established in Northwest Hydraulic and Rainbow Pipe Line (1999), the failure or rejection of a hypothesis still constitutes a valid technological advancement because proving that a hypothesized pathway does not work advances general technological understanding and reinforces the measure of the technological uncertainty.

Under the "How" Requirement, the claimant must demonstrate how the work is being conducted: it must be carried out by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The CRA's Guidelines specify four mandatory elements that constitute a systematic investigation or search: (i) the generation of a hypothesis—an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving a problem; (ii) the testing of this idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, recognizing that the hypothesis may evolve and change as testing progresses; (iii) the development of logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (iv) the keeping of evidence generated as the work progresses.

Crucially, taxpayers must not mistake the CRA's simplified "Why" and "How" Guidelines for a relaxation of the common law test. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (affirming 2019 TCC 246) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), appellants argued that because neither subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act nor the CRA's August 2021 Guidelines explicitly contain the phrase "scientific method," the Tax Court erred in applying the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected this contention in both appeals, ruling that CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts, that Element 1 of Northwest Hydraulic is embedded in the "Why" requirement while Elements 2 through 5 are summarized within the "How" requirement, and that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the binding judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1).
2.3 Delineation of Support Work under Paragraph 248(1)(d) and Excluded Work under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Once an SR&ED project satisfies the core eligibility criteria of basic research, applied research, or experimental development, Step 2 of the analysis determines the boundary of eligible tasks within the project. Under paragraph 248(1)(d), support work means work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where—and only to the extent that—such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED unless linked to qualifying core SR&ED in Canada (with a specific statutory accommodation for non-arm's-length contractors performing support work, addressed in Section 4.5).

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven statutory categories of work ("excluded work"), which can never be claimed as SR&ED even if performed during a broader product development cycle:

items: Market research or sales promotion (paragraph (e));
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (paragraph (f));
Research in the social sciences or the humanities (paragraph (g));
Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (paragraph (h));
The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (i));
Style changes (paragraph (j)); and
Routine data collection (paragraph (k)).

body.text: 3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Mechanics: Pool of Deductible Expenditures and Investment Tax Credits
3.1 Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada accumulate their allowable SR&ED expenditures in a cumulative tax account known as the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (computed in Part 3 of Form T661, Line 455).

The Section 37 pool is increased each taxation year by: (1) allowable current SR&ED expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada—comprising eligible salaries or wages, materials consumed or transformed, contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant, third-party payments to approved entities, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, and (where the Traditional Method is elected) directly related and incremental overhead expenditures; (2) allowable capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; (3) repayments made in the year of government or non-government assistance that had previously reduced the pool; (4) SR&ED ITC amounts recaptured in the prior taxation year; and (5) pool balances transferred upon an amalgamation or wind-up. Conversely, the pool is decreased by government assistance (including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, unless renounced by the filing due date) and non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing due date, as well as amounts deducted from the pool in previous years (on Schedule T2SCH1, Line 411) and amounts deducted in respect of insolvency. Notably, while a contract payment received by an SR&ED performer reduces the performer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(18), it does not reduce the performer's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

Deducting an amount from the Section 37 pool in a given taxation year is optional for corporations, individuals, and trusts. Any undeducted balance in the pool may be carried forward indefinitely to future taxation years, allowing loss-making or pre-revenue businesses to defer claiming SR&ED deductions until they become profitable. However, three statutory restrictions govern the Section 37 pool:

items: Loss Restriction Event (Subsection 37(6.1)): If a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), the undeducted pool balance is restricted and may not be fully deducted in that year or subsequent years unless specific continuity-of-business and income-streaming rules are met.

Partnerships (Subsection 96(1)): A partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance to a subsequent fiscal period; the entire pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income or loss for the year.

Exclusion of Acquired Rights: Under Section 4.0 of the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, no deduction is allowed under section 37 for an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing a patent or technology rights), ensuring that only the performer of the SR&ED claims the tax incentive without duplication.

body.text: 3.2 Section 127 and 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Refundability, and Carryover Rules

While the Section 37 pool governs income deductions, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool (calculated in Part 4 of Form T661, Line 570, and reported on T2 Schedule 31 or Form T2038(IND)) determines the taxpayer's Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under subsection 127(9). The qualified expenditure pool is calculated at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over to subsequent years. However, once earned, any non-refundable (or non-refunded) SR&ED ITC must first be applied against Part I tax otherwise payable (Schedule 31, Line 560), after which any unused ITC balance may be carried back 3 taxation years (Schedule 31, Lines 911, 912, and 913) or carried forward 20 taxation years, expiring if unapplied after 20 years. As established in Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen (2001), the taxpayer may elect the order in which credits are deducted.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026) and Bill C-15, the applicable ITC rate (35% enhanced vs. 15% basic) and cash refundability rate (100%, 40%, or 0%) depend on the claimant's legal structure, whether the qualified expenditures are within or above the annual expenditure limit, and whether the expenditures are current or capital in nature:

Budget 2019 eliminated previous-year taxable income from the SR&ED expenditure limit calculation for CCPCs, leaving prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada—or, post-December 15, 2024, the elective three-year average gross revenue test—as the sole phase-out mechanism for the expenditure limit.)
3.3 Annual Expenditure Limit ($6 Million Cap) and Phase-Out Formulas (Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue)
The annual expenditure limit determines the maximum dollar volume of qualified SR&ED expenditures on which a CCPC or (post-December 15, 2024) an ECPC can earn the enhanced 35% ITC.
A. Pre-Reform Taxable Capital Formula (Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024)

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only CCPCs were eligible for the 35% enhanced rate, up to a maximum expenditure limit of $3,000,000. The expenditure limit began to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada (as defined in the Income Tax Act and explained in archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532, Part I.3 – Tax on Large Corporations) of the CCPC and any associated corporations for the preceding taxation year reached $10,000,000, and became nil at $50,000,000:

In this formula, A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is less than or equal to $10,000,000, or is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000 in any other case.
B. Post-Reform Taxable Capital Formula for CCPCs (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit increases to $6,000,000, and the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds expand to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out span):

In this formula, A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated group) is less than or equal to $15,000,000, or is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000, eliminating the expenditure limit at $75,000,000.
C. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the 3-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 expands access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC (up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three statutory conditions: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Even if all shares owned by non-residents were hypothetically owned by a single particular person, an ECPC must still not be controlled by that particular person. In addition, Canadian-resident corporations where all or substantially all (≥90%) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are eligible for the refundable ITC.

An ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000:

In this formula, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which the three-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000. For corporations that are members of a corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is the amount reported in the group's annual financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation, and group members must share the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (including the average annual revenue of each group member for the preceding three fiscal years regardless of whether they were associated during the entirety of that period). For non-group corporations, gross revenue is the amount reported in the corporation's GAAP annual financial statements presented to shareholders.

Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC (or a group of associated CCPCs) may elect to calculate its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure instead of the taxable capital structure. This election allows capital-intensive private corporations (such as life sciences, clean-tech, or hardware ventures with high paid-up capital or debt exceeding $15 million but low or nil revenue) to preserve their full $6,000,000 expenditure limit.
3.4 Associated Corporations, De Facto Control, and Partnership Allocation Rules

Associated CCPCs must share the annual expenditure limit and file T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026) to allocate the limit among group members. Where a corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 365 days), or where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC, subsection 127(10.5) prorates the corporation's allocated expenditure limit by the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365. For example, as illustrated in Section 3.1.2 of the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if Corporation P is allocated $3,000,000 of the group limit and has a second short taxation year running 184 days from July 1 to December 31, 2027, its expenditure limit for that short year is $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,328.

To qualify as a CCPC under subsection 125(7) (or as an ECPC), the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by non-residents or (for CCPCs) public corporations. Under section 256 of the Income Tax Act, control encompasses both de jure voting control and de facto control (factual control or undue operational/financial influence, as examined in HSC Research, 1995; Mimetex Pharmaceutical, 1999; Mindready Solutions, 2015 CCI 17; Aeronautic Development Corp., 2017 TCC 39; and CO2 Solution Technologies, 2019 CCI 286).

When SR&ED work is performed by a partnership, the ITC is calculated at the partnership level and allocated to eligible partners (individuals, corporations, or trusts) at the end of the partnership's fiscal period under subsection 127(8) and the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy. As confirmed in All Colour Chemicals (CTC), the partnership allocation rule in subsection 127(8) overrides the CCPC enhanced rate in subsection 127(10.1): partnerships earn SR&ED ITCs strictly at the 15% basic rate, meaning qualified CCPCs should avoid performing SR&ED inside a partnership structure if they wish to access the 35% enhanced ITC rate.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Election Methods, and Capital Property Restoration
4.1 Salaries and Wages, Directly Engaged Personnel, Specified Employee Caps (YMPE), and the 10% Foreign Work Rule

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment under the Income Tax Act (T4 remuneration). It includes base salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's or management fees, commissions, inducement or non-competition payments, taxable benefits under section 6 (where there is a cash outlay or a reasonable estimate of actual non-cash costs excluding recoverable GST/HST/PST and not claimed elsewhere as a business expense), and—for non-specified employees only—bonuses and remuneration based on profits. Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages exclude the employer's share of related payroll benefits (e.g., CPP, EI, employer pension contributions, health benefits), extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits under section 7 (disallowed for taxation years after November 14, 2005, following Alcatel, 2005 TCC 149), retiring allowances, and remuneration not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year.
A. "Directly Engaged" Employees (Proxy Method) vs. Traditional Method Wages

Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada can be claimed. "Directly engaged" refers to hands-on technical tasks determined by the actual duties performed rather than job title: performing experiments and engineering analysis, preparing equipment and materials for tests (excluding routine maintenance), collecting data, recording measurements, making calculations, writing experimental computer programs, and performing eligible support work. First-line supervisors and managers qualify as directly engaged only for the time spent directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED activities or providing direct technical input; non-technological management, budgeting, and supervision beyond the first-line level are excluded. Clerical and administrative staff (accounting, payroll, HR, purchasing, reception, legal support) are never considered directly engaged under the Proxy Method. Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)), however, a claimant may also claim administrative and clerical salary or wages (as well as the employer's share of related benefits and retiring allowances for SR&ED staff) as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360, provided they satisfy the "directly related" and "incremental" tests. Under both methods (including Regulation 2900(5) for the Proxy salary base), if an arm's-length (non-specified) employee spends all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of their time on eligible SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be for SR&ED.
B. Statutory Caps on "Specified Employees"

A "specified employee" is an employee who is a specified shareholder—owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the claimant under section 251 (such as a relative of a controlling shareholder). Specified employees are subject to four strict limitations across direct SR&ED wages and the Proxy salary base:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: All bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from both direct SR&ED wages and the Proxy salary base.

Maximum 75% Time Allocation Cap: The ASA (90% = 100%) deeming rule does not apply to specified employees; claimable salary or wages for a specified employee cannot exceed 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages (after excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages).

Direct SR&ED Salary Ceiling — 5 Times YMPE: For direct SR&ED expenditure purposes, the maximum salary or wages claimable for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed (and shared among associated corporations on Form T1174).

Proxy Salary Base Ceiling — 2.5 Times YMPE (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): For calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661, the salary base inclusion for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of 75% of total eligible salary or wages and 2.5 times the YMPE prorated for the number of days employed in the taxation year (shared among associated corporations):

body.text: C. The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule and the 10% Foreign SR&ED Labour Rule

Under section 78 (subsection 78(4)) of the Income Tax Act, any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days from the end of that taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year. They must be excluded from that year's claim (reported on Line 315 of Form T661) and can only be claimed as direct SR&ED wages in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (Line 310), although prior years' unpaid wages paid in a current year are permanently excluded from the Proxy salary base. Similarly, current expenditures other than salary or wages (such as contractor or material invoices) unpaid within 180 days of year-end are deducted on Line 520 of Form T661 when computing qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, and are added back (at 100% or 80%, as applicable) in the subsequent year when paid.

For SR&ED work performed outside Canada, expenditures generally do not enter the Section 37 pool or earn ITCs (though foreign current R&D expenses may be deducted under subsection 37(2) in computing business income). However, under Section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada are deemed to be incurred in Canada (qualifying for both the Section 37 pool and federal ITCs) up to a maximum of 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages carried on inside Canada in that year, provided four conditions are met: (1) the work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (not a subcontractor); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work was related to a business of the claimant; and (4) the foreign work was solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant.
4.2 Overhead and Other Expenditures: Traditional Method vs. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method
Claimants must make an annual, irrevocable election on Form T661 between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method for calculating SR&ED overhead and other expenditures.

Most Canadian SR&ED claimants elect the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) because it requires no tracking or allocation of actual overhead items. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026), the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the salary base (the PPA rate was 65% prior to 2013, 60% in 2013, and has been 55% since 2014). For any employee (whether a specified employee or a regular arm's-length employee), the salary base under Regulation 2900(9) excludes: (1) bonuses, (2) remuneration based on profits, (3) taxable benefits under section 6, (4) stock option benefits under section 7, (5) prior years' unpaid salary or wages paid in the year (Line 310), and (6) employer-paid related benefits. The PPA is included in qualified expenditures solely to earn the SR&ED ITC; it is not added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures because the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA are already deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations, the PPA is subject to an overall cap calculated by the formula A − B − C, which ensures that total SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specified statutory deductions do not exceed total business deductions for the year:

items: A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold);

B is the total of deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (CCA, interest, bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED pool deduction on Schedule T2SCH1, Line 411), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development), and Section 104 (trusts); and
C is the total expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (rent).

body.text: Conversely, under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Regulations), no PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant itemizes, tracks, and allocates actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Form T661, Line 360, which enter both the Section 37 deductible pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, each claimed overhead expenditure (or rational, non-arbitrary portion thereof) must satisfy two cumulative tests:

items: Directly Related Test: The expenditure must have a direct linkage to the specific SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or machinery/equipment used to perform SR&ED, with no intervening step or intermediary.

Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Eligible items include clerical/administrative salaries providing direct support to SR&ED staff, the employer's share of related benefits for hands-on SR&ED employees, non-SR&ED trade contracts (e.g., electricians, welders, mechanics modifying an experimental setup), utilities directly consumed by SR&ED equipment, domestic travel and training for SR&ED staff, scientific periodical subscriptions, clinical trial volunteer fees, and SR&ED health and safety costs. Fixed monthly telephone/cellular/internet rates, post-project waste disposal, and prescribed non-eligible costs (SR&ED claim preparation fees, convention/conference attendance costs, and interest expenses) are excluded.

body.text: 4.3 Treatment of Cloud Computing, Hosting, and Software Licences

The eligibility of cloud computing costs (such as R&D compute clusters and AI model training infrastructure) and software subscriptions depends strictly on the expenditure classification and the overhead method elected:

items: Ineligible as SR&ED Materials: Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials must be physical, tangible substances in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state that compose the body of a thing on which SR&ED is performed. Cloud compute, hosting, data, and software subscriptions are intangible and cannot be claimed as materials consumed or transformed.

Disallowed Separately under the Proxy Method: Under the Proxy Method, cloud computing and software subscription expenses are treated as overhead already represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4). Claiming cloud or software subscription invoices separately while electing the Proxy Method constitutes double-counting and is disallowed on audit.

Claimable as Overhead under the Traditional Method: Where a compute-intensive business (such as an AI or data analytics firm) incurs incremental R&D cloud computing expenses that exceed 55% of its proxy salary base, electing the Traditional Method allows the company to claim the R&D cloud infrastructure costs as actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360, provided the claimant maintains separate cloud accounts segregating R&D/experimental development infrastructure from commercial production hosting and proves the compute costs were directly related and incremental to the SR&ED work.

Outright Software Acquisitions After December 15, 2024: Under the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), computers and outright acquisitions of computer software or licences/rights to use computer/systems software after December 15, 2024, that fall within prescribed CCA classes and are used all or substantially all (≥90%) for SR&ED over their expected useful life may qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures.

body.text: 4.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture Rules

Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy, a claimant can claim the cost of physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or component parts that compose the body of a thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process, claimed in the taxation year the material is actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED (and paid within 180 days of year-end). Materials consumed are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless—retaining less than 10% of their original cost as scrap or residual value—as a result of the SR&ED. Materials transformed are materials incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom product, or experimental production run that retains 10% or more of its value after testing. Lab supplies (beakers, petri dishes, pipettes, filter papers), cleaning supplies, cutting tools, lubricants, and general utilities do not compose the body of the experimental object and cannot be claimed as SR&ED materials.

Under subsections 127(27) to (36) of the Income Tax Act and the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, ITC recapture rules apply whenever a taxpayer sells or converts to commercial use a property (or another property incorporating the property) on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed—specifically materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), or physical property acquired through an SR&ED contract. Consumed materials (even if sold as scrap for <10% of cost) are not subject to recapture. Crucially, as illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a corporation manufactures an experimental part in-house, there is no recapture on the in-house salaries or overhead used to build the part (only the cost of transformed materials is subject to recapture); whereas if the corporation orders the part from an arm's-length supplier for $12,000 ($10,000 manufacturing/development cost plus $2,000 profit), the entire $12,000 cost is subject to ITC recapture upon commercial conversion or sale.
4.5 Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length Subcontractors (80% Rule) and Third-Party Payments to Approved Entities

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), subsection 127(9), and the Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, when a claimant engages an arm's-length taxable supplier to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf (where the payer controls the work and holds exclusive rights to the results), 100% of the eligible contract cost enters the Section 37 deductible pool, while 80% of the expenditure qualifies to earn SR&ED ITCs (with 20% deducted on Line 529 of Form T661). Payments made in respect of an SR&ED contract to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier (e.g., a foreign contractor with no Canadian permanent establishment) are completely excluded from qualified expenditures on Line 528. For the arm's-length Canadian contractor, the amount received or receivable is a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) that reduces the contractor's own qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18), preventing duplicate ITC claims unless the contractor incurred excess SR&ED costs at its own financial risk (Com Dev Ltd., 1999).

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (section 251), paragraph 127(9)(f) excludes the payer's contract outlay from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (though it remains in the payer's Section 37 deductible pool). Instead, the payment is not treated as a contract payment to the NAL performer, who may either claim the ITC directly on its own underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures or file Form T1146 (updated May 15, 2026) jointly with the payer to transfer those qualified expenditures to the payer. Additionally, under Section 7.4 of the CRA policy, a NAL performer may claim standalone support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)) performed for a related payer's core Canadian SR&ED project.

Distinct from SR&ED contracts, third-party payments (reported on Form T1263 and Form T661, Line 370, and governed by the Third-Party Payments Policy) are payments made to A Entities (Canadian-resident corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1), earned in the year the SR&ED is performed), B Entities (approved associations), C Entities (approved universities, colleges, or research institutes), D Entities (tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j)), E Entities (granting councils such as CIHR, NSERC, and SSHRC under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)), or F Entities (non-profit SR&ED corporations performing basic/applied research under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)). To qualify, the SR&ED must be carried on in Canada, be related to a business of the claimant, and the claimant must be entitled to exploit the results of the research; 80% of an eligible third-party payment qualifies for the SR&ED ITC.

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nine provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits that stack alongside the federal SR&ED program; only Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (unless renounced by the taxpayer on or before the income tax return filing due date) constitute "government assistance" for federal income tax purposes, reducing both the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and federal qualified expenditures for ITC calculation.
5.1 Québec: The New Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) and Abolished Legacy Credits

In the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget, Québec's Minister of Finance introduced the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation), administered by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec). Effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC replaces Québec's fragmented legacy credits with a single, consolidated 100% refundable tax credit.

Under the CRIC regime, a qualified corporation (or corporate member of a qualified partnership) with an establishment in Québec earns an increased refundable rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures incurred in Québec above the applicable exclusion threshold, and a basic refundable rate of 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 limit. Unlike Québec's former R&D salary tax credit (which provided 30% on the first $3.0 million for CCPCs and 14% for non-CCPCs or above $3.0 million), the 30% CRIC rate on the first $1,000,000 is available to all qualified corporations regardless of their total assets or revenue, with associated corporations sharing the $1,000,000 limit on Form RD-1029.8.EN-T. For each taxation year or fiscal period, eligible expenditures must first be reduced by an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of (1) $50,000 or (2) the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold. The CRIC is claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization activities) and is taxable for Québec income tax purposes in addition to reducing the federal SR&ED pool.

Crucially, the CRIC expands Québec's eligible base beyond traditional SR&ED to include both pre-commercialization activities—defined as tests, technological validations, studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements, and product/industrial design that constitute a continuation of R&D activities undertaken in Québec by or on behalf of the taxpayer—and capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property used in Québec R&D or pre-commercialization, alongside salaries and wages, subcontractor fees (50% inclusion for arm's-length subcontractors), and payments to eligible research organizations. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC eliminates seven legacy Québec tax measures: (1) the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (s. 1029.7, Form RD-1029.7); (2) the tax credit for university research or public research centres/consortia (s. 1029.8.6, Form RD-1029.8.6); (3) the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; (4) the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; (5) the tax credit for technological adaptation services; (6) the industrial design component of the design tax credits (while preserving the fashion design component); and (7) the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. Additionally, for Québec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI), the Québec nexus ratio for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, is calculated using R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (excluding pre-commercialization expenditures and without reduction by the CRIC exclusion threshold).
5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario offers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered jointly with the CRA through the T2 return:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Sections 38 to 45 / Section 96, T2 Schedule 566): An 8% fully refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 annual refund, entered on Schedule 5, Line 468). The $3,000,000 limit is shared across associated corporations and phases out when the associated group's prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 and/or when prior-year taxable paid-up capital ("specified capital amount") is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 (with compounding reductions if both thresholds are exceeded).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45, T2 Schedule 508): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (entered on Schedule 5, Line 416), with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward period (Note: the CRA's provincial summary table lists 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward for ORDTC alongside schedule instructions). Because the 8% OITC is treated as government assistance for ORDTC purposes, the ORDTC is computed on the Ontario expenditure pool after deducting the OITC, resulting in a combined effective Ontario credit rate of 11.22% ($80,000 OITC + $32,200 ORDTC on $1,000,000 of spend). However, because claiming the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC immediately grinds the federal SR&ED pool, pre-profit CCPCs with no Ontario income tax payable often renounce the ORDTC by the filing due date under subsection 127(19) to avoid reducing their 35% federal cash refund.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — T2 Schedule 568): A 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible research contract with an approved Ontario university, college, or hospital/non-profit research institute, up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (maximum $4,000,000 refundable credit). Neither OITC, ORDTC, nor OBRITC reduces the OITC base, though all claimed Ontario credits reduce the federal SR&ED pool.

body.text: 5.3 Western Provinces: British Columbia (2026 Permanent & ECPC Expansion), Alberta (IEG), Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

In British Columbia (Income Tax Act (BC), sections 97 to 103, claimed on Form T666 within an absolute 18-month filing deadline), corporations with a permanent establishment in BC earn a 10% refundable SR&ED tax credit on annual qualified BC expenditures up to the federal expenditure limit ($6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, previously $3,000,000; maximum $600,000 refund) and a 10% non-refundable credit on expenditures above that limit or for non-qualifying corporations (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward). In BC Budget 2026, British Columbia made the BC SR&ED tax credit permanent (eliminating its September 1, 2027 sunset date), enhanced the credit, and extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) in alignment with the federal program.

In Alberta (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, sections 26.95 to 26.99, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within a strict 15-month filing deadline after fiscal year-end), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a fully refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible Alberta R&D spending. The IEG pays an 8% base rate on eligible spending up to the corporation's "base level of spending" (defined as the average of the corporation's qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the prior two years) and an enhanced 20% rate (8% base + 12% incremental) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that two-year average base.

In Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan), sections 63 to 63.4, T2 Schedule 403), CCPCs earn a 10% refundable R&D tax credit on up to $1,000,000 of annual eligible Saskatchewan expenditures (maximum $100,000 cash refund; note that while some informal summaries list $100,000 as the limit, $100,000 is the maximum credit generated by the statutory $1,000,000 expenditure cap), and a 10% non-refundable credit on CCPC expenditures above $1,000,000 and for all other corporations (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward). In Manitoba (The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), section 7.3, T2 Schedule 380, 12-month filing deadline), corporations earn a 15% R&D tax credit on eligible Manitoba expenditures: for in-house R&D, half (7.5%) is refundable and half (7.5%) is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward), whereas R&D carried out in Manitoba under contract with a qualifying educational institution is 100% refundable at the full 15% rate and 100% of the educational contract payment is eligible (exempt from the 80% subcontractor cap).
5.4 Atlantic Provinces and Northern Territories: New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon

All four Atlantic/Northern jurisdictions with R&D tax credits provide 15% fully refundable credits with no corporate size restrictions or expenditure caps. New Brunswick (New Brunswick Income Tax Act, section 59, T2 Schedule 360) and Nova Scotia (Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), section 41, T2 Schedule 340, 18-month filing deadline) each provide a 15% fully refundable credit to corporations with a permanent establishment in the province. Newfoundland and Labrador (Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), section 42, T2 Schedule 301 for corporations and Form T1129 for individuals, 12-month filing deadline) provides a 15% fully refundable credit whose eligible expenditure base is uniquely not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits). Yukon (Income Tax Act (Yukon), T2 Schedule 442 for corporations and Form T1232 for individuals, filed within 12 months of the filing due date) provides a 15% fully refundable credit on eligible Yukon R&D expenditures, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 6. Direct Innovation Grants, Government Assistance Interactions, and Stacking Mechanics
6.1 Major Federal Direct R&D Funding Programs (NRC IRAP, SIF, Global Innovation Clusters, NSERC Alliance, Mitacs)

Beyond retrospective SR&ED tax credits, Canadian businesses frequently stack prospective direct grants and contributions administered by federal innovation agencies. The foundational direct grant program for small and medium-sized enterprises is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which supports incorporated, for-profit Canadian businesses with 500 or fewer staff conducting R&D in Canada. Engaged prior to incurring project costs through an Industrial Technology Advisor (ITA), NRC IRAP provides non-repayable contributions reimbursing up to 80% of internal technical salaries and up to 50% of contractor fees (typical awards run up to $1.0 million, with a median award around $75,000 and a $10.0 million ceiling, plus a dedicated $100,000–$1.0 million clean technology stream and up to $50,000 for IP strategy and execution under IP Assist, which received a $75 million three-year extension in Budget 2025).

For large-scale industrial R&D and collaborative commercialization, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (contributions up to $50 million) and Global Innovation Clusters (such as NGen for advanced manufacturing and the Ocean Supercluster, offering up to $5 million). In the November 4, 2025 federal budget, the government announced that ISED will wind down certain legacy funding envelopes in the Global Innovation Clusters and the SIF Net Zero Accelerator, reallocating new direct funding toward dual-use defence technologies ($656.9 million over five years), critical minerals processing ($443.0 million over five years with Natural Resources Canada), quantum technology ($334.3 million through the Defence Industrial Strategy), sovereign space launch capability ($182.6 million), and the $1.0 billion Venture and Growth Capital Catalyst Initiative. For industry-academic collaborations, NSERC Alliance Grants fund 66.7% (two-thirds) of direct university research costs ($20,000 to $1.0 million annually for 1 to 5 years) against a 33.3% (one-third) corporate cash contribution, while Mitacs Accelerate matches a company's $7,500 contribution to fund a $15,000 four-to-six-month graduate research internship unit (or $10,000 corporate contribution toward a $20,000 postdoctoral unit).
6.2 Statutory Reduction of Qualified Expenditures: Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under subsections 127(18) to (20) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, any government assistance (subsection 127(9)—grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, provincial tax credits, or super-allowance benefit amounts from a government, municipality, or public authority, including COVID-19 wage subsidies such as CEWS), non-government assistance (paragraph 12(1)(x)—inducements or reimbursements from private entities), or contract payment (subsection 127(9)) in respect of SR&ED that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date must reduce the claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis.
Two statutory rules govern how assistance interacts with the SR&ED calculation:

items: Project-by-Project Isolation and Non-Arm's-Length Allocation (Form T1145): Assistance received for a specific project reduces only the SR&ED expenditures of that project; it cannot reduce the expenditures of an unrelated SR&ED project, nor can it reduce a project's pool below zero (any excess assistance above the project's expenditures is included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x)). Where assistance is shared across non-arm's-length corporate group members performing the SR&ED, Form T1145 (updated May 15, 2026) may be filed to allocate the assistance. When previously deducted assistance is repaid in a later year, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool and earns an ITC at the rate that would have applied in the original year the assistance reduced the pool.

Preservation of the Unreduced Proxy Salary Base: Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, direct wage grants (such as NRC IRAP) and provincial tax credits do not reduce the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). The 55% PPA is computed on the full eligible directly engaged SR&ED salary base first, and the grant or provincial tax credit is deducted subsequently from total qualified expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661.

body.text: 6.3 Bill C-69 "Excluded Loans" Exception and Mathematical Stacking Examples (Federal + Provincial + Grant)

Prior to 2024, low-interest or repayable innovation loans from government bodies were held to constitute "government assistance" (as seen in CAE, 2022), forcing borrowers to reduce their SR&ED expenditure pool by the entire loan principal upon receipt. Under Bill C-69 (Royal Assent June 20, 2024, effective retroactively to January 1, 2020 for loans made after December 31, 2019), subsection 127(9) was amended to exclude "excluded loans" (defined in subsection 12(11) as bona fide loans with reasonable repayment terms from public authorities in Canada) from government assistance, allowing companies to stack repayable public innovation loans with SR&ED without pool grinding.

body.text: 7. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Administration
7.1 Institutional Roles: Department of Finance Canada, CRA, and ISED

Three federal institutions govern Canada's R&D incentive system (alongside Revenu Québec and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration for non-harmonized provincial credits). The Department of Finance Canada designs statutory tax policy, initiates legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (such as Bill C-15 and Bill C-69), and approves special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program and eight harmonized provincial/territorial credits through its SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), conducting technical eligibility reviews and financial audits. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) and the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) oversee direct discretionary R&D grant programs including SIF, Global Innovation Clusters, and NRC IRAP.
7.2 Mandatory Prescribed Forms and the Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, as set out in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and T2 Schedule 31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals/trusts) containing all prescribed information on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline.

The SR&ED reporting deadline is defined strictly as 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of its taxation year (when a tax year ends on the last day of a month, the T2 return is due on the last day of the 6th month and the SR&ED reporting deadline falls on the last day of the 18th month). For trusts, the T3 return is due 90 days after the trust's tax year-end, making the SR&ED reporting deadline 12 months and 90 days after year-end. Under subsection 220(2.2) (enacted November 17, 2005, overriding Alex Parallel Computers), the Minister has no statutory authority or discretion to extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline. If a claimant fails to submit Form T661 or Schedule 31—or omits mandatory prescribed fields—by the 18-month deadline, the expenditures are permanently disallowed as SR&ED and no ITCs can be earned (as strictly enforced in Datacalc Research, 2000; Easyway Cattle, 2015 TCC 211; Westsource, 2017 TCC 9; and Fooi, 2024).

body.text: 7.3 Form T661 Line-by-Line Architecture (May 2026 Revision) and Claim Preparer Penalties

Under the May 15, 2026 revision of Form T661 (reflecting Bill C-15) and the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, claimants must complete Parts 1 through 10. Part 1 captures general claimant data and the irrevocable overhead method election. Part 2 (Project Information — Sections A, B, and C) requires project-by-project technical narratives written by personnel familiar with the scientific or technical work. On the May 15, 2026 form, Part 2 includes Line 207 (first 5 digits of the Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 Field of Research code, RDF#####), Lines 212 and 214 (pre-claim approval indicator and case number), Line 262 (names of up to 10 of the most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024, claimed on Line 390 for each project), Line 263 (percentage of total operating time used in SR&ED for each property on Line 262), Line 266 (parties contracting the claimant), and Lines 267 to 269 (subcontractors). Claimants with more than 20 projects may submit Part 2 with their return for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided they report the costs of every claimed project in Part 6 and maintain completed Part 2 descriptions for all remaining projects at their place of business for immediate submission upon CRA request.

Part 3 calculates allowable SR&ED expenditures (Line 400, including Lines 350/355 for post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases, Line 360 for Traditional overhead, and Line 390 for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures) and the Section 37 deductible pool (Line 455). Part 4 calculates total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes on Line 570 (adding the PPA on Line 502 and SUE on Line 504, and deducting unpaid non-salary amounts on Line 520, non-taxable supplier contracts on Line 528, the 20% contract/third-party reduction on Line 529, and prescribed/other deductions on Lines 530–535). Part 5 computes the proxy salary base, the 55% PPA (Line 820), and the overall cap. Part 6 allocates project costs across all claimed projects (including Box 759 for post-December 15, 2024 leased equipment costs and Box 780 naming the 20 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties or SUE acquired after December 15, 2024). Parts 7, 8, and 10 cover statistical reporting, the claim checklist, and officer certification.

Uniquely, Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information)—which requires disclosing every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim, alongside billing arrangements—is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline: missing, incomplete, or inaccurate information in Part 9 will not result in disallowance of the SR&ED claim, but triggers a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable. Conversely, under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act, false statements or plagiarized technical narratives made knowingly or under gross negligence trigger civil penalties and allow the CRA to reopen statute-barred taxation years (as confirmed in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc., 2025 TCC 173), while criminal SR&ED fraud convictions carry fines of 150% to 300% of the amount claimed (R v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018).
7.4 CRA Technical and Financial Review Process and the Elective Pre-Claim Approval Program

Under the November 2025 federal budget and the CRA's 2026 administrative rollout, the CRA introduced an optional pre-claim approval process and updated its claimant guidance in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (replacing The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants), alongside upgrades to the SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT). Through the pre-claim approval service, eligible businesses can submit planned R&D projects before work starts or costs are incurred and receive an upfront eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks, entering their pre-claim approval indicator and case number on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661 upon filing. Post-filing reviews evaluate technical compliance with subsection 248(1) and financial substantiation of contemporaneously tracked project expenditures.
8. Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Judicial Precedents (1998–2026)
8.1 Foundational Appellate Authorities: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

The bedrock of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), in which Judge Bowman established the five-question test for SR&ED eligibility, recognized "system uncertainty" in complex engineering models (allowing 4 of 5 projects), and held that the failure or rejection of a hypothesis constitutes a valid technological advancement. The Federal Court of Appeal adopted and affirmed Northwest Hydraulic as binding appellate law in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA)—holding that obtaining a new product or patent does not excuse the absence of documentary or factual proof of systematic experimentation—and in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA).
8.2 Appellate Reaffirmation of the Scientific Method and Expert Independence: Kam-Press Metal and National R&D

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)—citing earlier appellate rulings in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2011 TCC 261) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 152 (aff'g 2015 TCC 186)—the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal involving 3D CAD modelling and factory floor mock-ups of curved glass-and-metal memorial niche columns. Justice Webb held that moving the definition of SR&ED from the Income Tax Regulations to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act did not alter the legal standard, and that adherence to the scientific method (Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic) remains mandatory even though those exact words do not appear in the statute.

One year later, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed the denial of SR&ED credits for a dynamic SQL database software project where the taxpayer satisfied Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty) but failed Criteria 2 through 5. The FCA established two major evidentiary and substantive precedents: first, the Tax Court properly refused to qualify the taxpayer's proposed external expert witness because the taxpayer's sole shareholder/president had written 65% of the proposed expert's report and the report improperly acted as an advocate offering legal conclusions on SR&ED eligibility, violating the Experts' Code of Conduct; second, the CRA's August 2021 "Why/How" Guidelines do not displace Northwest Hydraulic, and a taxpayer cannot introduce technical articles on appeal to argue an unproven distinction between the "engineering method" and the "scientific method" that was not established through expert evidence at trial.
8.3 Contemporaneous Documentation, Credible Oral Testimony, and Software/Engineering Rulings (Les Abeilles, Joel Theatrical Rigging, Dazzm, Willowglen Systems)

In Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, the Tax Court of Canada allowed four process-development projects despite sparse written records because the employees who performed the work gave highly credible, detailed oral testimony proving systematic hypothesis testing. Equally important, the Court ruled that the Crown's proposed expert witness—the CRA internal staff member who had denied the claim—was not sufficiently independent or impartial, observing his confusion between defending CRA administrative policies and an expert witness's overriding duty to assist the Court impartially. Conversely, in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed claims for a theatre fire-curtain hydraulic speed-control system and a stage-curtain manual override crank, holding that shop-floor trial-and-error without engineering analysis fails Criteria 1 to 4, and that "Experiment Summary Sheets" drafted retroactively after project completion by an external tax consultant do not satisfy Criterion 5.
Recent 2024–2026 Tax Court decisions have clarified the application of Northwest Hydraulic to modern software, food science, and industrial engineering:

items: Dazzm Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129: Allowed a cloud-based SaaS claim where integrating open-source tools (React and Redux) created systemic performance uncertainties beyond routine debugging or standard optimization, endorsing a holistic evaluation of software projects supported by metrics and testimony.

Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7: Delivered a landmark split decision in industrial control software—allowing the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control box project based on cumulative "system uncertainty" not resolvable by available methods, while disallowing $1,293,692 for the SCADACOM-5 project because software modernization and scale-up using known tools constitutes commercial product development rather than experimental development.

Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC): Allowed an SR&ED claim for developing a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar/cold-pressed drink ("Chrisoda") using novel High Pressure Processing (HPP) parameters, holding that technological uncertainty can exist even when standard chemical preservatives are publicly known if they cannot be used in the specific context, and that contemporaneous records (pH and microbial counts) need only track hypotheses, tests, and results for practitioners in the field.
